answer: Admission runs on hardware-minted identity pearls. To join, a machine presents a secure enclave whose monotonic counter never read before; it seals a kernel of attested state into the registration, and the registry stores that counter, refusing a second identity from the same one. Counter capacity is physically bounded per chip, so each puppet needs its own enclave: no bulk discount, cost grows linearly with N, while an honest operator pays once. If one inlet floods with mismatched counters, the registry throttles only unproven entries.
